Ki’lian’s character is notably devoid of pity. His narcissism is profound, leading him to perceive the world as revolving around his own interests; this delusion serves to mask the insecurities etched into his flesh beneath the dark layers he covets. As her nails dig into his hand, a grimace crosses his features, tightening his expression and lending severity to his jaw. Yet, despite the palpable tension, a grin never fully fades from his lips. He neither releases her nor increases the pressure, but simply holds her in place.

"Chores can wait," he states. "There is plenty more of you to fill your absence for a few minutes."

Such words are unlikely to inspire confidence, nor do they suggest that he intends to keep her there and submit her to an eternity of misery, a state the dragon seems to embody. Ki’lian does not intend for his remarks to be reassuring. When her politeness becomes ridiculous, the Bronzeryder warns, "Don't lie to me." He sounds more bemused than threatening, even though his entire demeanor maintains a menacing aura. "That typically does not end well for anyone. If you truly cannot think straight with a dragon nearby, so be it."

Since its establishment in 1949, NATO has played a critical role in maintaining transatlantic security and shaping post-war international order. The alliance has promoted political, economic and military cooperation among its member states. However,  in recent years, NATO has faced growing internal tensions regarding burden-sharing, alliance cohesion and the credibility of US security commitments (Badawi & Zreik, 2025). These tensions have intensified during Donald Trump’s first term in office. Trump took a more transactional stance towards NATO, criticized allies for insufficient defence spending, questioned the credibility of the NATO Article 5 commitments, and even suggested the possibility of US withdrawal (Ringsmose & Webber, 2020). These shifts generated significant concerns about the cohesion and credibility of NATO and have forced the EU to rethink NATO’s strategic direction (Badawi & Zreik, 2025).  Despite facing the same changes in US alliance leadership and operating under the same transatlantic security framework, European states have pursued divergent defence strategies. While some states promoted greater strategic autonomy and the development of independent defence capabilities, others prioritized preserving the long-standing transatlantic security bond. Additionally, some countries pursued a hedging strategy that strengthened both NATO commitment and European defence cooperation (Schreer, 2019). The coexistence of such different strategic responses to the same external influences form the central empirical puzzle of this research. From a theoretical perspective, this divergence challenges the structural realist assumption that countries exposed to common systemic stimulus should pursue relatively similar defence strategies. This puzzle is situated in a broader academic discussion about alliance politics, transatlantic security and European defence cooperation. Existing literature has examined transatlantic tensions, changes in US alliance leadership and debates about European strategic autonomy. Scholars have also identified several explanations for divergent European defence responses, including geopolitical proximity to Russia, strategic culture and institutional dynamics at the EU level. However, these explanations are often examined separately, either with a focus on individual countries or on EU-level developments. Current literature therefore provides limited explanations of how the common systemic stimulus are interpreted and transformed into different national defence policies. Additionally, most existing literature focused on transatlantic tensions during Trump’s first term. Even though Trump's second administration began in January 2025 and continues to reshape the transatlantic security context, little attention has been paid to the influence of his NATO stance on the current European national defence strategies. Trump’s return to the White House is particularly important because it transforms previous concerns about the alliance reliability from a temporary political uncertainty into a more enduring systemic context, further promoting European states to reevaluate their defence and alliance strategies. This suggests the need for a more integrated and comparative analysis of divergent European responses.

The preparation and the presentation itself were significantly more time consuming than expected, but in return I gained a deeper understanding of what effective communication really means.  From choosing a topic to speaking in front of the class, I recognized many of my strengths and potential areas for improvement. I was able to easily find material on my topic of “Healthy Hygeine” and felt confident when I presented it in my speech. The structuring also worked surprisingly well. After the research, I was able to organize the most important points and create a coherent presentation. However my time management was catastrophic. I squeezed all the exercises and final adjustments into the very last minute which made me unnecessarily nervous. The easiest thing was the research and brainstorming. Since I like to learn new things, gathering information and selecting the material was easy for me. Conversely, the most difficult aspect was the practice and the actual lecture to speak in front of an audience, which is not easy for me since I get nervous quickly speaking infront of large crowds.  It was incredibly difficult to memorize everything without sounding monotonous. What I enjoyed the most was summarizing the lecture content and creating the visual aid and seeing everything come all together into a finished presentation. This gave me a great sense of accomplishment.  On the other hand, I was surprised at how quickly time passed during the lecture. I thought my presentation was quite good in the end, explained the main points well, and the prepared materials supported my lecture. However I do wish I had made more eye contact and spoke more confidently. I noticed that my pace and pitch were inconsistent in places due to my nervousness, I was nervous when the lecture began. I gradually got used to it as I spoke and was relieved and a little proud when it was over.  If I could do it again, I would spend more time practicing loudly and if possible practicing in front of someone to gain more confidence. For the actual presentation, I would speak more slowly and focus on controlling my nervousness.  It was also incredibly educational, watching my fellow peers present and listen to their speeches. My peers inspire me being confident, keeping eye contact and speaking calmly and clearly. They also put in materials effectively and underlined the content without interrupting the lecture. Speeches that were simply read from a script or slides, on the other hand, were completely uninteresting. If the voice is too quiet or the ideas are unstructured it is incredibly hard to follow and stay intersted.  Overall, this experience showed me that public speaking is a skill that is very useful. I now know how public speaking works and what I still need to work on. I plan to approach my next presentation with more confidence and preparedness.

Since 1970, the U.S. stock market has experienced five major crashes: the stock market crash in 1973/74, Black Monday in 1987, the burst of the dot-com bubble in 2000-2002, the global financial crisis in 2007-2009, and the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020. These historical events tell us that great turmoil in financial history is not unusual, but a recurring phenomenon that occurs periodically. When investor confidence disappears and the market outlook changes, although each crash has different direct triggers, crashes tend to be more frequent when macroeconomic conditions deteriorate, asset prices are overly optimistic, and the financial system loses stability. Section I: Introduction and Research Design

The assumption that financial globalization would reduce the incidence of conflict had been based on the premise that financial globalization would increase the costs of armed conflict. However, in international political economy literature, the implication of this type of globalization has been shown to be asymmetric forms of coercion. The move by the Group of Seven (G7) countries to freeze Russia's foreign exchange reserves and cut off Russian banks from the SWIFT network represented a watershed moment for international politics and economy, marking a shift towards weaponizing financial interconnectivity and raising the spectre of security implications for Chinese authorities as they observe the impact of this measure on the Russian economy.

China’s sensitivity to this type of action arises from its exposure to Western financial choke points. As a result of China’s integration into a global trading system that is built upon the US dollar, Beijing faces a dilemma of sorts, whereby it must maintain open economic channels with the West for economic growth and development, while at the same time preparing its banking system and state reserves against the possibility of Western interference.

Main Research Question

How much has the emergence of alternative payment channels and bilateral liquidity arrangements reduced the exposure of China to Western financial pressure?

Variables and Their Operationalization

To answer the main research question posed above, this proposed project sets out to identify the causal links between three independent variables and one primary dependent variable:

Dependent variable: The degree of China’s vulnerability to G7 sanctions as measured by the proportion of China’s transactions that are routed through banks or messaging systems under Western control.

Independent variable 1: The volume of transactions carried out through the Cross-Border Interbank Payment System (CIPS), the Chinese clearinghouse that utilizes the ISO 20022 messaging format. This variable captures the extent to which CIPS can operate independently from the SWIFT network.

Independent variable 2: The availability and drawdown rate of bilateral currency swap facilities, under the administration of the People’s Bank of China, that are shielded from sanctions. This variable reflects the level of liquidity that is accessible through these facilities and the speed with which funds can be accessed in a non-aligned network.

Independent variable 3: The volume of strategic multilateral assets that have been re-invoiced. This variable tracks the quantity of vital energy supplies and basic commodities being purchased in renminbi and settled via alternative ledgers.

Research Objectives

This research proposal develops a conceptual framework to assess China’s ability to counter Western financial pressure through alternative channels. To accomplish this aim, the research will achieve the following objectives:

Investigate how CIPS facilitates the separation of CIPS-maintained messages from messages that are dependent on SWIFT.

Analyze how China’s trade partners deal with the friction associated with China’s capital controls to obtain security guarantees.

Assess whether multi-central bank digital currency projects create corridors that circumvent US-controlled correspondent banks.

Hypothesis

China’s alternative infrastructure is defensive in nature rather than acting as a mechanism to pursue monetary hegemony. The Chinese Communist Party (CCP) is content to sacrifice the benefits of a global reserve currency as such status would entail opening the capital account, the establishment of an independent legal system, and the opening up of domestic bond markets to foreign investors. Instead, it seeks political control at home and constructs a parallel financial system to secure its supply chains. The goal of establishing parallel channels is to safeguard China’s physical supply chain in times of crisis by deliberately giving up the advantages associated with being a global reserve currency.

This proposed project integrates two fields of international political economy that have historically been treated separately: the analysis of network vulnerabilities in centralized infrastructures and the study of the macroeconomic foundations of monetary supremacy. Through their synthesis, the project reveals an area of theoretical neglect pertaining to how a secondary power in a highly integrated system establishes an alternative structure while also maintaining its participation in the dominant global system.

1. Weaponized Interdependence and Network Vulnerabilities

The concept of weaponized interdependence argues that states have the capacity to leverage asymmetrical, centralized global networks to exert coercive influence, thereby challenging the conventional wisdom that high levels of economic interdependence deter war (Farrell & Newman, 2019; Keohane & Nye, 1977). States that hold jurisdiction over central nodes utilize two principal mechanisms: the Panopticon Effect and the Chokepoint Effect. The former refers to the ability of nodes to monitor the flow of information and material across the entire network, while the latter pertains to the capability of nodes to isolate specific actors from the rest of the network (Farrell & Newman, 2019). Because states that manage financial technology servers and regulate transnational communication infrastructure maintain jurisdiction over them, they possess the capability to track the transaction records of non-domestic entities.

When applied to the global financial system, the two mechanisms correspond to the Society for Worldwide Interbank Financial Telecommunication (SWIFT) and the Clearing House Interbank Payments System (CHIPS), respectively. SWIFT operates on US-based servers. CHIPS is headquartered in New York City, making it subject to US regulatory oversight. Consequently, Washington is positioned to exert considerable influence over financial activities.

Trade rules are employed to coerce governments into hyper-liberalizing data flows, thereby stripping local public authorities of their autonomy to govern transnational entities. Additionally, these conditions must ensure that people retain their right to vote and participate in the democratic process. The WSIS provides a foundation based on human rights, as well as intersectional and feminist frameworks, to address the geopolitics of global inequality and injustice. Ultimately, the conclusive test of a well-guided digital transition lies in the public, collective, and social value it creates, and the human freedoms it expands.
